The prefix be- is itself an old loan into Norwegian from Middle Low German be- and German be-. The verb drite continues Old Norse dríta (“to defecate”), from Proto-Germanic *drītaną (“to defecate”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreyd- (“to have diarrhea”).

en.g: Charon; the largest of the five known moons of the dwarf planet Pluto
x: Charon og Pluto vender alltid samme side mot hverandre.
Charon and Pluto always face the same side toward each other.
Charon er den største av Plutos måner.
Charon is the largest of Pluto's moons.

1000293.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from English Charon (“Charon, Pluto's largest moon”). The astronomical name was proposed by American astronomer James W. Christy after his discovery of the moon in 1978. Christy formed the name partly in reference to Char, the nickname of his wife Charlene, and partly after the mythological Charon, the ferryman of the underworld. The latter association was particularly appropriate for a moon of Pluto, since Hades, the Greek ruler of the underworld, corresponds to the Roman god Pluto.
The mythological English name is ultimately from Latin Charōn (“Charon, ferryman of

en.g: Umbriel; the third-largest moon of Uranus, discovered by William Lassell in 1851 and named after the character Umbriel in Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock
x: Umbriel har en mørk og sterkt kraterfylt overflate.
Umbriel has a dark and heavily cratered surface.
Umbriel er en av Uranus' 27 kjente måner, og ble oppdaget i 1851 av den britiske astronomen William Lassell (1799–1880).
Umbriel is one of Uranus's 27 known moons, and was discovered in 1851 by the British astronomer William Lassell (1799–1880).

1001061.etyen:
Internationalism, based on English Umbriel, the name of a gloomy gnome created by Alexander Pope for his poem The Rape of the Lock (1712). Pope formed the name from Latin umbra (“shadow, shade”).
The moon was discovered together with Ariel by William Lassell on 24 October 1851. The names of the four then-known moons of Uranus were suggested by John Herschel in 1852 at Lassell's request. Umbriel was chosen after Pope's “dusky, melancholy sprite”.
Compare the parallel adaptations Danish Umbriel, Swedish Umbriel, German Umbriel, Dutch Umbriel, French Umbriel, Polish Umbriel and English Umbriel.

1001317.etyen:
A spelling variant of Sven, with doubled final n; ultimately from Old Norse Sveinn m, originally a byname based on the common noun sveinn (“boy, young man, servant”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Svenn, Danish Svenn and Swedish Svenn (“male given name”).

1003621.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from Italian a battuta (“in strict time; with the beat”), literally “to the beat”. The first element a (“to, at, with”) is from Latin ad (“to, towards, at”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”). Italian battuta (“beat, measure”) is a deverbal noun formed from the feminine past participle of battere (“to beat, strike”), inherited from Latin battere (“to beat, strike”), from earlier battuere (“to beat, strike”), of uncertain ultimate origin.
Compare the parallel borrowings Danish a battuta, Swedish a battuta, German a battuta, French a battuta, Estonian a b

1003877.etyen: grøft + -e- + fyll, first part from Old Norse grǫftr (“digging, burial”), from Proto-Germanic *graftuz (“digging, carving”), from *grabaną + *-þuz, first part from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrobʰ-, o-grade form of Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to dig, scratch, bury”). Last part from Old Norse fylla (“to fill, complete”), from Proto-Germanic *fullijaną (“to fill, make full”), from *fullaz + *-janą, first part from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós, from *pleh₁- (“to fill”).

The hospital organized a professional development day on patient safety for its employees.
Driv – Senter for kvinnehelseforskning inviterer deg til en inspirerende fagdag viet til kvinnehelseforskningens mangfold og bredde.
Driv – Centre for Women's Health Research invites you to an inspiring professional development day devoted to the diversity and breadth of women's health research.

1004901.etyen:
From fag (“subject, field”) + dag (“day”), literally “subject day”.
The first element, fag (“subject, field, discipline”), is borrowed from Middle Low German fak (“compartment, field”), originally referring to something joined together or a delimited area, and later developing the senses “field, discipline” and “school subject”. The second element, dag (“day”), is inherited from Old Norse dagr (“day”) and is related to døgn (“24-hour period”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk fagdag, Danish fagdag and German Fachtag (“professional conference day”).
